overview: Rise 5.99's TargetStrafe steers the player around the Kill Aura target by rewriting the movement yaw the client's movement code uses. Where the Memeware variant drives the strafe axis, the Rise variant rotates the direction itself: within range the module sets the patched EntityPlayer.movementYaw to the target yaw plus or minus a 78-degree offset, so the player orbits at the configured range, and beyond range it sets the yaw straight at the target to close the gap. Direction changes are decided by a block probe five ticks ahead, horizontal collision and ground checks, with jump-only and manual-direction options on top.

sections.p:
The module hooks onStrafe, which Rise's patched movement code fires while computing the player's motion each tick. The handler reads Aura.target, the shared kill-aura target, and the Range number setting, then computes getYaw: the angle to the target's extrapolated position, using the difference between the target's current and last-tick positions. It writes the result into EntityPlayer.movementYaw, a static field added by Rise's runtime patch. MoveUtil consults that field in every strafe and direction helper, and the patched player movement code applies it, so the whole client steers the motion to the module's yaw.

The settings wrap the core: jumpOnly makes the module steer only while the jump key is held, clearing movementYaw otherwise and restoring the third-person view; controllable lets the left and right keys force the orbit direction; thirdPerson switches the camera while active. onDisable clears movementYaw and resets the tick counter, so a disabled module leaves no steering state behind.

Within range the module writes yaw plus 78 plus twice the distance error, or yaw minus the same value depending on direction. At exactly the configured range the offset is 78 degrees, which puts the motion roughly tangential to the target vector; when the player drifts inside the range the offset shrinks and when they drift outside it grows, steering the orbit back to the configured radius. The direction flip is governed by ticksSinceLastInverted: the module probes the block five ticks ahead along the current movement direction, and flips when that block is not air or the player is collided horizontally, and also when there is no block under the probe and the Fly module is off, with that last condition gated so it only acts after more than one tick since the previous flip.

The probe uses MoveUtil.getDirection with the current movement yaw, then PlayerUtil.getBlockRelativeToPlayer at five times the current speed along that direction. The controllable setting overrides the direction decision from the keyboard, and the distance comparison uses the player's actual distance to the target, so the approach and orbit phases share one state machine.

onRender3DEvent draws a circle around the target at the range setting minus 0.5 blocks, using the theme color, whenever the jump key is held or jumpOnly is off. The circle is visual only; the walked orbit radius is governed by the 78-degree offset and the distance correction. Aura coordinates through the same movementYaw field: with its silent-rotation and strafe settings enabled it writes the server yaw there, and it nulls the field otherwise, so the two modules share one steering channel rather than owning separate ones.

files.label: TargetStrafe.java (orbit module)
files.explanation:
The module is a single onStrafe handler plus render code. It resolves the target from Aura.target, reads the range setting, and computes the yaw to the extrapolated target position with Math.atan2. The distance check decides between approach and orbit: beyond range the movement yaw is the plain target yaw, inside range it is the target yaw offset by 78 degrees plus a distance correction that grows or shrinks as the player drifts.

The direction state machine is the other half. ticksSinceLastInverted counts ticks since the last flip. The flip fires when the block probe five ticks ahead lands in a non-air block, when the player is collided horizontally, or when there is no ground under the probe and the Fly module is off, with that last condition gated so it only acts after more than one tick. The probe reads the movement direction through MoveUtil.getDirection, which first substitutes the current movementYaw, so it tests the direction the player will actually move.

The render handler draws the ring at range minus 0.5 and the module restores the third-person view and clears the movement yaw when the jump-only gate closes or the target disappears. onDisable clears the yaw and the counter. The module never constructs a packet; the steering state it writes is consumed by the patched movement code, so its wire presence shows up only in the C03 stream and the C0B sprint state of the surrounding movement.

files.label: MoveUtil.java (steering consumer)
files.explanation:
MoveUtil is the consumer side of the steering channel. The strafe helpers begin with the player's yaw and substitute EntityPlayer.movementYaw whenever it is non-null, then apply the 90-degree strafe-key offsets and the backward 180-degree flip before producing motionX and motionZ from the sine and cosine of the resulting angle. getDirection(yaw) performs the same substitution for direction consumers, which is what the module's block probe uses.

Because every helper applies the movementYaw substitution, the patched movement code and the module agree on one direction source. The same field is how Aura implements silent rotations: it writes the server yaw there when its strafe and silent-rotation settings are enabled, and nulls it otherwise, so the field is a shared steering register rather than a module-private variable.

The module's orbit math and the utility's consumption are what make the 78-degree offset visible on the wire: the player moves along the substituted yaw while the packet yaw is the aim rotation, so the angle between the reported facing and the motion is roughly 78 degrees plus the distance correction.

countering.label: Strafe (45-degree motion angles)
countering.explanation:
Hawk's Strafe check validates the angle between the player's acceleration direction and the reported yaw. It takes the angle modulo 45 degrees and requires the remainder to land within 0.5 degrees of a multiple of 45, which are the only angles a legitimate keyboard strafe can produce: straight, 45-degree diagonals, sideways and backward. The check runs only for grounded players with at least two consecutive position updates, and excludes teleports, knockback, collisions, jumps and liquids.

The 78-degree base offset is exactly the failure case this check is built around. When Rise's silent rotations report the aim yaw, the server sees motion at 78 degrees plus the distance correction off the facing, and 78 is not a multiple of 45: the remainder is 33 degrees, which is 12 degrees away from the nearest multiple, far past the 0.5-degree threshold. The violation rubberbands the player, which snaps the orbit center and breaks the circle.

The correction term does not save the module: as the distance error changes, the offset sweeps between roughly 72 and 84 degrees, and none of those values are multiples of 45. The only configurations that avoid the check are one where the client does not report the aim rotation, which defeats the kill aura's silent aim, and one where the player faces the motion direction, which defeats the point of orbiting while facing the target.

countering.label: SprintDirection (sprint motion vs yaw)
countering.explanation:
SprintDirection scores the sprinting player whose motion diverges from the reported yaw. It requires the sprint flag to have been up for at least two consecutive ticks and a horizontal move of at least 0.2 blocks, then measures the angle between the yaw vector and the move vector, with friction, soul sand, web and hit-slowdown adjustments applied to the expected force. An angle above about 62 degrees is a violation with a rubberband.

Rise's orbit runs with the sprint flag up whenever the player holds W, which is the normal way to use it, and the movement yaw puts the motion at roughly 78 degrees from the reported aim yaw, far past the 62-degree limit. The check is entirely server-side: it reads the move packets and the reported rotation, so the client-side movement yaw never enters the decision, and the fact that the orbit is generated by a steering field rather than a strafe key is invisible to it.

The same honest boundary applies as in the Memeware variant: without the sprint flag the check skips the player, so a walk-speed circle with sprint off is not scored here. The sprinting orbit is the configuration the module is normally used in, which is what makes this check a practical counter rather than a theoretical one.

countering.label: SurvivalFly (movement envelope + illegal sprint)
countering.explanation:
NCP's SurvivalFly validates every move against a physics envelope built from the world and the previous move's momentum. The horizontal allowance is the friction-decayed previous speed plus the input force the motion implies, and anything above it raises a violation that ends in a set-back. The envelope includes the sprint multiplier, the jump stage, slime, ice and stair modifiers, so the check models the full range of legitimate ground and air motion.

TargetStrafe changes direction, not speed, so the envelope's target is the velocity the orbit inherits. A grounded orbit at walk speed sits inside the envelope, while an orbit driven by a speed module above the walking model accumulates horizontal distance above the limit and is set back, breaking the circle. In the jump-only mode the check bounds the airborne leg of the orbit with the jump-stage allowance, so sustained sprint-jump circling at over-speed is scored the same way as any bunny-hop.

The illegal-sprint input cross-check adds the direction dimension on servers that know the client's WASD impulse: a sprinting player whose impulse reads backward is tagged illegalsprint and reset, which covers the reversal ticks when the orbit flips direction and the movement yaw swings behind the facing. The envelope covers speed on every server; the input check covers the direction contradiction where the impulse is known.

countering.label: Speed (base speed envelope)
countering.explanation:
Arc v2's Speed check measures the horizontal distance of each move against a base speed of 0.2873 blocks per tick adjusted for speed potions, with extra allowances for ice, slime blocks, stairs and jump stages. On the ground it averages the move over the accumulated ground ticks and flags when the move exceeds the base plus the average; in the air it compares against the base plus a stage constant and any pending knockback velocity.

The orbit holds a constant tangential speed, which is precisely the profile the on-ground accumulator is designed to measure. A legal-speed circle passes, while a circle driven at bunny-hop velocity keeps the average low and the instantaneous move high, tripping the on-ground expected branch with a set-back to the previous location. The jump-only mode feeds the air branch instead, which applies the same envelope with the stage constants for a jump.

The check has no direction component, so it cannot identify the orbit as such; it bounds the speed the orbit can carry. On servers running Arc v2 the target strafe is therefore limited to legal velocities, which is the same role the check plays against any movement module: it removes the speed half of the signature while the Hawk direction checks remove the geometry half.
